clue.text: Look carefully over the island for building material

parts.note: to con a text is to study it or look it over carefully
Crete, the large Greek island, here named as if the only one

explanation.surface: Someone inspects an island before choosing what to build with.
explanation.definitionFit: Concrete is the cement, sand and gravel mix poured to make walls and foundations.

clue.text: So Don is by Snow !

parts.note: a university lecturer wears a mortarboard at graduation, and a mountain top wears snow, so both are given a covering on top

explanation.surface: A man called Don is linked to a writer named Snow.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Don' and 'Snow' look like names (C. P. Snow wrote about dons) but are a university teacher and snow on a peak.
explanation.definitionFit: A don may wear a cap on ceremonial occasions, and a peak topped with snow is said to be covered on its top in the same word.

clue.text: Heraldic King of the North

parts.note: one of the English Kings of Arms has responsibility for heraldry north of the river Trent, and his title comes from the French for 'north king'

explanation.surface: A heraldic monarch reigning over northern lands.
explanation.walkthrough: The College of Arms has a Norroy King of Arms (now Norroy and Ulster) for the north; the name is Old French 'nord roy'.
explanation.definitionFit: The title of the King of Arms for northern England derives from Norman French for king of the north.

clue.text: Cain's upbringing ?

parts.note: to raise Cain is to cause uproar, so the child Cain's rearing shares a word with the idiom

explanation.surface: How Adam and Eve's son was brought up.
explanation.walkthrough: The idiom 'raise Cain' means make trouble; upbringing is another sense of the word.
explanation.definitionFit: Bringing up a child is rearing it, and the idiom for causing a commotion is to do the same to Cain.

clue.text: It comes with a west wind, in part

definitions.text: It comes with a west wind, in part

indicators.note: only part of the phrase with a west is used, the letters lying across its words

explanation.surface: Something that arrives on a westerly breeze.
explanation.definitionFit: Mild westerly winds bring a melting of ice and snow after frost.

clue.text: Western invitation to a personal viewing sometime

definitions.text: Western invitation to a personal viewing sometime

parts.words: Western invitation to a personal viewing sometime
parts.note: the film star Mae West's famous line invited a man to come and see her sometime; 'Western' means belonging to Mae West

explanation.surface: A cowboy asks someone round for a private showing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Western' suggests cowboys, but it means 'of Mae West', whose catchphrase was "Why don't you come up and see me sometime?"
explanation.definitionFit: The phrasal verb begins Mae West's invitation to visit and look her over.

clue.text: What prospect for the returning batsman?

definitions.text: What prospect for the returning batsman

parts.words: What prospect for the returning batsman
parts.note: a cricketer heading back to the pavilion has been dismissed, and what he sees ahead of him is a view while dismissed

explanation.surface: Asking what future awaits a cricketer coming back from injury.
explanation.walkthrough: A batsman returns to the pavilion when he is out, so his view is an 'out look'. 'Prospect' means view or outlook.
explanation.definitionFit: A prospect is a view ahead or what the future seems to hold, which this word means.

annotationWithheld.why: A flap, Sir Knight, for you? (8): PARSIFAL is an anagram of A FLAP SIR, but no clue word signals the anagram ('for you' is no indicator), as was common in old Times puzzles
annotationWithheld.clue: A flap, Sir Knight, for you?

clue.text: Landor announced that none was worth his !

definitions.text: Landor announced that none was worth his

parts.words: Landor announced that none was worth his
parts.note: Walter Savage Landor's quatrain begins 'I strove with none, for none was worth my' and the missing final word is the entry

explanation.surface: A poet boasts that no rival was worth his effort.
explanation.walkthrough: The poet Walter Savage Landor wrote 'I strove with none, for none was worth my strife'; the clue asks for that last word.
explanation.definitionFit: In Landor's line the word means conflict or struggle, the contest he would not stoop to.

clue.text: Umpire employed even when apparently turned down

parts.note: ref is short for referee, an official like an umpire
used means employed, put to work

explanation.surface: An umpire was hired even though he seemed to have been rejected.
explanation.definitionFit: Declined or rejected, as an offer that is turned down.

clue.text: Alien no longer concerned with the ear

parts.note: ex- means former, something that no longer is
otic is the anatomical adjective for things relating to the ear

explanation.surface: Someone stops worrying about an outsider's hearing.
explanation.definitionFit: Something foreign or from another land is strange, as an alien thing is.

clue.text: About to do a fast time that is to be sniffed at !

parts.note: re means about or concerning, as in business letters
Lent is the Christian season of fasting before Easter

explanation.surface: Someone about to run a quick time that critics will dismiss.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fast time' looks like a quick run; it is a season of fasting. 'To be sniffed at' looks like scorn, but it means smelled.
explanation.definitionFit: Something with a strong scent invites a sniff, which is what redolent means: smelling of something.

clue.text: Shakespeare's brood ?

parts.note: Ben Jonson called Shakespeare the Sweet Swan of Avon, so the playwright's offspring would be young swans

explanation.surface: The playwright's children.
explanation.walkthrough: Ben Jonson's tribute calls Shakespeare 'Sweet Swan of Avon'.
explanation.definitionFit: Young swans are what a swan's brood consists of, and Shakespeare was the Swan of Avon.

clue.text: Aylesbury flapper, a potential beauty-queen

parts.note: an Aylesbury is a breed of white duck, and a young one flapping its wings may grow up beautiful, like the swan in Andersen's tale

explanation.surface: A lively young woman from a Buckinghamshire town might become Miss World.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Flapper' suggests a 1920s girl, but it is a young bird; Aylesbury, a Buckinghamshire town, gives its name to a breed of duck. Andersen's plain chick grows into a swan.
explanation.definitionFit: Andersen's despised duckling became a lovely swan, so the phrase means someone plain who may blossom into beauty.

clue.text: Got a job and lodgings!

parts.note: a billet is both a job or post and a soldier's quarters, so one word covers getting work and getting housed

explanation.surface: Someone lands employment and somewhere to live at once.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Billet' means a position or job, and to be billeted is to be lodged, as soldiers in private houses.
explanation.definitionFit: Soldiers billeted on householders are given quarters, and a billet is also a post or job.

clue.text: Tea-maids turned nudists !

indicators.note: the letters of the phrase are turned about into a new order

explanation.surface: Women who serve tea take up naturism.
explanation.definitionFit: A Christian sect that worshipped naked, imitating Adam's innocence before the Fall.

clue.text: Americans call it a day !

parts.note: the Fourth of July holiday in the United States is named after this freedom, so Americans attach the word 'Day' to it

explanation.surface: Americans decide to stop work for the day.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Call it a day' usually means stop working; here it means that Americans name a holiday, Independence Day, after the word.
explanation.definitionFit: Freedom from British rule, declared in 1776, is celebrated by Americans on the Fourth of July.

clue.text: Gamblers who go into transports on water

definitions.text: who go into transports on water

explanation.definitionFit: Bettors are called this in Britain, and people who propel flat-bottomed river boats with poles share the word.

clue.text: Part of a musical barrow-load

parts.note: the Dublin song about Molly Malone has her wheeling her wheelbarrow and crying 'and mussels, alive, alive-o'

explanation.surface: Some of the goods on a singing street seller's cart.
explanation.walkthrough: In the song 'Molly Malone' she wheels her barrow crying 'cockles and mussels, alive, alive-o'.
explanation.definitionFit: Small edible shellfish that Molly Malone sold alongside mussels from her barrow.

clue.text: Pride's had a fall-out of the frying-pan ?

indicators.note: pride comes before a fall in the proverb, and here the letters fall into a new order

explanation.surface: Pride came before a fall, out of the frying-pan into the fire.
explanation.walkthrough: A spider is an old frying pan standing on three legs.
explanation.definitionFit: A long-handled frying pan on legs, used over an open fire, was called by the name of the eight-legged creature.

clue.text: Sailor in popular regard

parts.note: pop is short for popular, as in pop music
to eye something is to regard or look at it

explanation.surface: A seaman who is well liked.
explanation.definitionFit: The spinach-eating cartoon seaman created by E. C. Segar.

clue.text: Menial at sixes and sevens has to lay plates

indicators.note: to be at sixes and sevens is to be in confusion, so the letters are jumbled

explanation.surface: A muddled servant has to set the table.
explanation.walkthrough: 'At' serves inside the idiom 'at sixes and sevens' and also as fodder: MENIAL plus AT is rearranged.
explanation.definitionFit: To laminate is to build up or overlay in thin layers or plates.

clue.text: Africanus Major or Minor

parts.note: two Roman generals bore the title Africanus, the Elder and the Younger, and both shared one family name

explanation.surface: A Latin name in two sizes, like a pair of brothers at school.
explanation.walkthrough: Scipio Africanus the Elder defeated Hannibal; his adoptive grandson Scipio Aemilianus Africanus the Younger destroyed Carthage.
explanation.definitionFit: Both Roman generals called Africanus belonged to the family of the Scipios.

clue.text: One of the doggy few to disperse the foggy dew ?

definitions.text: One of the doggy few to disperse the foggy dew

parts.words: One of the doggy few to disperse the foggy dew
parts.note: the wartime system that burned fuel beside runways to clear fog had an acronym that is also a stock name for a dog; 'the few' recalls the RAF pilots

explanation.surface: A dog, one of a brave band, clearing a misty morning.
explanation.walkthrough: FIDO, Fog Investigation and Dispersal Operation, burned petrol along RAF runways in the Second World War; 'the few' were Churchill's Battle of Britain pilots.
explanation.definitionFit: The fog-clearing system was a classic dog's name, doggy in two senses.

clue.text: " In everything we are sprung Of Earth's first blood, have manifold " (Wordsworth)

definitions.text: In everything we are sprung Of Earth's first blood, have manifold

parts.words: In everything we are sprung Of Earth's first blood, have manifold
parts.note: a line of Wordsworth's sonnet on English liberty with one word missing after 'have'

explanation.surface: A quotation from Wordsworth with a gap to fill.
explanation.walkthrough: Wordsworth's sonnet 'It is not to be thought of' ends 'In everything we are sprung / Of Earth's first blood, have titles manifold.'
explanation.definitionFit: The missing word means claims or rightful honours, the manifold distinctions Wordsworth gives the English.

clue.text: Drive from the huntress's house

parts.note: Di is short for Diana, the Roman goddess of hunting, so this is Di's
a lodge is a small house, such as a gatekeeper's

explanation.surface: Being chased out of the home of a woman who hunts.
explanation.definitionFit: To force someone or something out of its place is to drive it away.

clue.text: Don't make a side turn to the street !

indicators.note: the word side is given a turn, its letters rearranged

parts.note: St is the standard abbreviation for street

explanation.surface: An instruction not to turn off into a side street.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Turn' reads like a driver's instruction, but it shuffles the letters of 'side' into DESI. 'Don't' alone is the definition, an order to stop.
explanation.definitionFit: An order to stop doing something, the same as telling someone to leave off.

clue.text: In short, she's constant and faithful, render it as you will

indicators.note: in short says the word constant is cut down to its opening letters

parts.note: true means loyal or faithful

explanation.surface: She is steady and loyal, however you interpret it.
explanation.definitionFit: To construe a passage is to translate or interpret it, to render its meaning.
